record.paper_title: Some Open Problems Related to Creative Telescoping
record.original_question: Given a proper hypergeometric term f(n, k) = p c^n d^k ∏_{i=1}^m Γ(α_i n + β_i k + γ_i)^{e_i}, where p ∈ C[n, k], c and d are in C, α_i, β_i, e_i are in N, and γ_i are in C, find a method to determine the removable and non-removable singularities of a telescoper for f using less computation than is required to compute a telescoper itself. Ask the analogous question for hyperexponential terms f(x, y) = exp(a/b) ∏_{i=1}^m p_i^{c_i}, where a, b, p_i ∈ C[x, y] and c_i ∈ C.

evidence.quote: Problem 3.3 (a) Find a way to determine the removable and non-removable singularities of a telescoper for a given proper hypergeometric term f(n, k) = pcndk ∏_{i=1}^m Γ(αin+βik+γi)^{ei} (p ∈ C[n, k], c, d ∈ C, αi, βi, ei ∈ N, γi ∈ C), using less computation time than needed for computing a telescoper. (b) The analogous question for hyperexponential terms f(x, y)= exp(a/b) ∏_{i=1}^m p_i^{c_i} (a, b, p_i ∈ C[x, y], c_i ∈ C).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A proper hypergeometric term in two discrete variables is a function of the form
  f(n,k) = p(n,k) · c^n · d^k · ∏_{i=1}^{m} Γ(α_i n + β_i k + γ_i)^{e_i},
where p ∈ C[n,k], c,d ∈ C, α_i, β_i ∈ N, e_i ∈ Z (with α_i, β_i, e_i nonnegative integers as specified), and γ_i ∈ C. A telescoper for f is a nonzero linear recurrence operator L(n, S_n) (with S_n the shift n ↦ n+1) such that L·f = Δ_k g for some hypergeometric term g, where Δ_k is the forward difference in k. The singularities of L are the roots of its leading coefficient as a polynomial in n; a singularity is called removable if there is another telescoper for f whose leading coefficient does not vanish there, and non-removable otherwise.

(a) Devise an algorithm that, given the data (p, c, d, {α_i, β_i, γ_i, e_i}) defining f, determines the removable and non-removable singularities of a telescoper for f using strictly less computational work than is needed to actually compute a telescoper.

(b) Solve the analogous problem in the continuous (hyperexponential) setting: a hyperexponential term is a function of the form
  f(x,y) = exp(a(x,y)/b(x,y)) · ∏_{i=1}^{m} p_i(x,y)^{c_i},
with a, b, p_i ∈ C[x,y] and c_i ∈ C, where a telescoper is a nonzero linear differential operator L(x, ∂_x) such that L·f = ∂_y g for some hyperexponential g. Determine, directly from the input data (a, b, {p_i, c_i}), which singularities of the telescoper are removable and which are not, with cost lower than computing a telescoper.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent literature on creative telescoping discusses Hermite-like reductions, additive/multiplicative decompositions, and existence criteria for telescopers of (mixed) hypergeometric and hyperexponential terms, but no algorithm is reported that predicts the removable and non-removable singularities of a telescoper directly from the input data more cheaply than computing the telescoper itself. The problem appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: On the existence of telescopers for mixed hypergeometric terms
status_evidence.snippet: A criterion for the existence of telescopers for mixed hypergeometric terms based on additive and multiplicative decompositions.
status_evidence.claim: Existence criteria are available, but singularity prediction at lower cost than computing telescopers is not addressed.

status_evidence.title: A Generalized Apagodu–Zeilberger Algorithm
status_evidence.snippet: Explicit upper bounds on the order of telescopers for proper ∂-finite functions.
status_evidence.claim: Bounds on telescoper order exist, but cheap prediction of removable/non-removable singularities is not provided.

status_evidence.title: Efficient Algorithms for Mixed Creative Telescoping
status_evidence.snippet: Hermite-like reduction procedure for bivariate hypergeometric-hyperexponential terms.
status_evidence.claim: State-of-the-art reductions still compute telescopers; no separate cheaper singularity-prediction algorithm reported.
